title: Transcendence is Preserved by Algebraic Operations: The Algebraic Numbers form a Subfield
description: Develops the arithmetic/field side of the algebraic–transcendental dichotomy, complementing the parent's countability result. For any field extension K ⊆ L, the elements algebraic over K form a subfield (algebraicSubfield K L), so the field of algebraic numbers is a countable subfield of ℂ. Dually, transcendence is preserved by every algebraic operation: if t is transcendental over K and a, b are algebraic over K, then t+a, a+t, t−a, a−t, t⁻¹, −t, tⁿ (n>0), a·t and t·a (a≠0), and the affine image a·t+b (a≠0) are all transcendental. A final contrast shows the transcendentals are NOT closed: t and 1−t are both transcendental but sum to the algebraic number 1.

overview.historicalContext: Cantor's 1874 result that the algebraic numbers are countable is a statement about cardinality. But the algebraic numbers carry far more structure: closed under the four field operations, they form the algebraic closure of ℚ inside ℂ — a countable algebraically-closed field. The elementary first half of that structure (closure under +, -, *, ⁻¹) is also the standard opening move of every concrete transcendence proof: once a single number such as e (Hermite 1873) is known transcendental, an entire algebraic orbit e+1, e², 1/e, 2e−3, … is transcendental for free. This entry isolates exactly that toolkit.
overview.problemStatement: Show that the elements of a field extension $K \subseteq L$ that are algebraic over $K$ form a subfield $\mathrm{algebraicSubfield}\,K\,L$ (so the algebraic numbers are a countable subfield of $\mathbb{C}$), and prove the dual statement that transcendence is preserved by every algebraic operation: if $t$ is transcendental over $K$ and $a, b$ are algebraic over $K$ then $t+a$, $t-a$, $t^{-1}$, $-t$, $t^n$ ($n>0$), $a\cdot t$ ($a\neq 0$) and the affine image $a\cdot t + b$ ($a\neq 0$) are all transcendental. Finally exhibit the structural contrast: $t$ and $1-t$ are both transcendental yet sum to the algebraic number $1$, so the transcendentals are no subfield.
overview.proofStrategy: Two halves. §1 (closure): the four ring operations are proved by rewriting IsAlgebraic to IsIntegral via isAlgebraic_iff_isIntegral (valid because K is a field) and invoking Mathlib's integral-closure subring lemmas IsIntegral.add/neg/sub/mul; inversion uses IsAlgebraic.inv. The six resulting lemmas are assembled into algebraicSubfield K L : Subfield L. §2 (preservation): each theorem is the contrapositive of a §1 lemma, discharged by a one-line back-substitution — e.g. if t + a were algebraic then t = (t+a) − a would be algebraic, contradicting transcendence of t; products use t = a⁻¹·(a·t) and so require a ≠ 0. transcendental_affine composes the additive and multiplicative cases. §3 (not closed): t + (1−t) = 1 is algebraic though both summands are transcendental.
overview.keyInsight: Transcendence preservation is the contrapositive of subfield closure. If t is transcendental and a is algebraic, then t + a cannot be algebraic, because otherwise t = (t + a) − a would be a difference of two algebraic numbers, hence algebraic — contradicting transcendence of t. The same one-line back-substitution (using a⁻¹ for products, inverses, etc.) handles every operation.
keyInsights: Transcendence preservation is the contrapositive of subfield closure: if t + a were algebraic with a algebraic, then t = (t+a) − a would be algebraic, contradicting transcendence of t. One back-substitution template (using a⁻¹ for multiplicative cases) proves every preservation theorem.

Over a field, algebraic equals integral (isAlgebraic_iff_isIntegral), so the deep fact that integral elements form a subring is reused verbatim for closure under +, −, ×; only inversion needs the separate field-specific IsAlgebraic.inv.

Inversion is the operation integrality alone cannot supply (1/2 is integral over ℤ, its inverse is not), but algebraicity over a field is closed under it: x⁻¹ is annihilated by the reversed polynomial of x.

The transcendentals are the set-theoretic complement of the algebraic subfield, and the complement of a nontrivial subfield is closed under no field operation — which is exactly why t and 1−t can both be transcendental while their sum 1 is algebraic.

transcendental_affine says the transcendentals are invariant under the whole algebraic affine group t ↦ a·t + b (a ≠ 0, a,b algebraic): from one known transcendental (e, π, a Liouville number) an infinite orbit of transcendentals follows for free.
overview.significance: Complements the cardinality/measure/category leaves of this family with the algebraic structure. It upgrades 'the algebraic numbers are a countable set' to 'a countable subfield', and it explains precisely why the transcendentals are NOT a subfield (closed under no field operation): they are the complement of a subfield.

sections.title: §1: The algebraic numbers form a subfield
sections.summary: Closure of algebraicity under +, -, *, neg and ⁻¹, packaged as algebraicSubfield K L : Subfield L. The four ring operations are proved by rewriting IsAlgebraic to IsIntegral (valid since K is a field) and invoking Mathlib's integral-closure subring lemmas; the inverse uses IsAlgebraic.inv.
sections.mathContext: For a field extension K ⊆ L the integral and algebraic elements coincide. Mathlib already proves the integral elements form a subring (IsIntegral.add/sub/mul/neg), and that the inverse of an algebraic element of a field extension is algebraic, so all six subfield axioms are available.

sections.title: §2: Transcendence is preserved by algebraic operations
sections.summary: Eleven preservation theorems: additive translates (t+a, a+t, t−a, a−t), nonzero rescalings (a·t, t·a), inversion (t⁻¹), negation (−t), positive powers (tⁿ), and the capstone affine map a·t+b. Each is a one-line contradiction from §1's closure lemmas.
sections.mathContext: These are exactly the closure facts the algebraic toolkit supplies to transcendence theory: the set of transcendentals is invariant under every algebraic affine map x ↦ a·x + b with a ≠ 0 and a, b algebraic.

sections.title: §3: The transcendentals are NOT closed
sections.summary: transcendentals_not_add_closed: for any transcendental t, both t and 1−t are transcendental, yet t + (1−t) = 1 is algebraic. The transcendentals therefore form no subfield — they are the complement of the algebraic subfield of §1.
sections.mathContext: The asymmetry is structural: the algebraic numbers are a subfield, the transcendentals are its complement, and a complement of a nontrivial subfield is never closed under the field operations.

sections.title: §4: Sanity checks over ℚ ⊆ ℂ
sections.summary: Concrete instantiations at K = ℚ, L = ℂ for an arbitrary transcendental t: t+1, t⁻¹, t², and 1−t are transcendental — demonstrating the general theorems on the field of complex numbers.
sections.mathContext: Witnesses for such t are guaranteed by the sibling leaves (uncountably many transcendental reals/complexes); classical examples include e and any Liouville number.

conclusion.summary: Beyond being a countable set, the algebraic numbers form a subfield of ℂ (algebraicSubfield), and transcendence is preserved under every field operation — addition/subtraction by an algebraic, multiplication/division by a nonzero algebraic, inversion, negation, positive powers, and arbitrary algebraic affine maps a·t+b. Dually, the transcendentals are closed under none of these: t and 1−t are transcendental but sum to the algebraic number 1. The algebraic numbers are the subfield; the transcendentals are exactly its complement.
conclusion.futureWork: Strengthen algebraicSubfield to an IntermediateField and prove it is algebraically closed (the algebraic closure of ℚ in ℂ); connect the affine-orbit structure to concrete transcendence statements such as Lindemann–Weierstrass (e^{α} transcendental for nonzero algebraic α).

mainTheorems.name: algebraicSubfield
mainTheorems.description: The elements of L algebraic over K, assembled as a subfield of L. Instantiated at K = ℚ, L = ℂ it is the field of algebraic numbers, which the parent proves countable.

mainTheorems.name: transcendental_affine
mainTheorems.description: For a ≠ 0 and a, b algebraic over K, the algebraic affine map t ↦ a·t + b sends every transcendental to a transcendental. Packages the additive and multiplicative preservation results.
mainTheorems.leanType: Transcendental K t → IsAlgebraic K a → IsAlgebraic K b → a ≠ 0 → Transcendental K (a * t + b)

mainTheorems.name: transcendental_add_algebraic
mainTheorems.description: A transcendental plus an algebraic is transcendental, by the back-substitution t = (t + a) − a.
mainTheorems.leanType: Transcendental K t → IsAlgebraic K a → Transcendental K (t + a)

mainTheorems.name: transcendental_algebraic_mul
mainTheorems.description: A nonzero algebraic times a transcendental is transcendental, by t = a⁻¹ · (a · t).
mainTheorems.leanType: Transcendental K t → IsAlgebraic K a → a ≠ 0 → Transcendental K (a * t)

mainTheorems.name: transcendental_inv
mainTheorems.description: The inverse of a transcendental element is transcendental.
mainTheorems.leanType: Transcendental K t → Transcendental K t⁻¹

mainTheorems.name: transcendentals_not_add_closed
mainTheorems.description: The transcendentals form no subfield: t and 1−t are transcendental, yet their sum 1 is algebraic.
mainTheorems.leanType: Transcendental K t → Transcendental K (1 - t) ∧ IsAlgebraic K (t + (1 - t))

mainTheorems.name: isAlgebraic_mul
mainTheorems.description: Product of algebraic elements is algebraic (one of the four subfield-closure lemmas), via integral closure.
mainTheorems.leanType: IsAlgebraic K x → IsAlgebraic K y → IsAlgebraic K (x * y)
